read: full: main text pp. 1-13 and appendices A-H pp. 16-22 read; appendix I (PRM visualisations, pp. 23-29) and the reference list skimmed
venue_now: ICLR 2024 (poster) according to notes/cited_set_resolution.md; the text file is arXiv 2305.20050v1, 31 May 2023 (page 1 footer) and shows no venue itself. The May reference list prints it as an arXiv preprint.
what_it_is: An OpenAI study comparing outcome supervision (feedback on the final answer only) with process supervision (human feedback on each intermediate step) for training reward models that pick the best of N sampled solutions to MATH problems (pp. 1-3). Human labelers marked each step of solutions from a GPT-4-based generator positive, negative or neutral, up to the first wrong step, giving PRM800K: about 800K step labels on 75K solutions to 12K problems (pp. 4, 6, 17, 19). The process-supervised reward model (PRM) solves 78.2% of a 500-problem MATH test subset in best-of-1860 selection, against 72.4% for the outcome-supervised model (ORM) and 69.6% for majority voting (p. 7); small-scale ablations that use the large PRM as a synthetic labeler, and an active-learning result (2.6x data efficiency), complete the study (pp. 8-9). It is a training-signal and reward-model paper, not a benchmark: reward models are scored by the final-answer accuracy of the solution they select (p. 3).
domain: competition mathematics (MATH); an out-of-distribution check on AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics and AMC10/12 questions (p. 10)
size: PRM800K: about 800,000 step labels over 75,000 solutions to 12,000 problems after filtering; 1,085,590 labels over 101,599 solutions unfiltered (pp. 4, 17). Test: 500 held-out MATH test problems, 1,860 samples per problem (pp. 5, 7, 18). OOD: 224 questions per the text but 234 per Table 1 (p. 10). Reward models fine-tuned from base GPT-4 (large scale) and from models with about 200x less pretraining compute (small scale) (p. 3).
source_of_items: existing problems (the MATH dataset; recent AP and AMC exams for the OOD check); the labelled solutions are samples from a fixed generator model, chosen by active learning to be convincing wrong-answer solutions (pp. 4-5, 10)
instances: static (MATH problems; solutions are model samples, but the problems are neither generated nor perturbed)
has_gold_traces: partial: human step-level correctness labels (positive, negative, neutral) on model-generated solutions, stopping at the first negative step in phase 2 (pp. 4, 6, 19). Labelers saw the ground-truth final answer but no reference solution (p. 19); no gold reference trace is used in evaluation.
evaluation: final answer: each reward model selects the best of N generator samples and the selection is graded automatically by its final answer (p. 3); no step-level classification accuracy of the reward models is reported. The step labels are training data, not an evaluation target.
human_validation: labeler quality control only: a 30-question screening test requiring at least 75% agreement with the researchers' gold step labels, then 10-20 quality-control problems per generation used to remove labelers whose quality slipped (pp. 17-18). No inter-annotator agreement figure is reported. The authors acknowledge that final-answer grading occasionally misgrades solutions (p. 5).
contamination_measures: string-matching and n-gram decontamination of the MathMix pretraining data against the MATH test split, with no strong guarantee claimed (pp. 11, 16); an OOD check on AP and AMC questions released after the pretraining data was compiled (p. 10); 4.5K MATH test problems were moved into training, so only 500 are held out (pp. 4-5, 18)

engtrace_use.sentence: Inspired by recent advances in process supervision (Lightman et al., 2023) and cascaded model verification (Chen et al., 2023), we introduce a two-stage evaluation framework that validates intermediate reasoning steps in addition to final-answer accuracy through a tiered verification protocol. (section 4, L390-395)
engtrace_use.explanation: For this paper the sentence claims only that process supervision is a recent advance that inspired step-level checking, and the paper supports that: it defines process supervision as feedback on each intermediate reasoning step (p. 1), shows that it trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision on MATH (78.2% against 72.4% best-of-1860, p. 7; at every data scale in the small-scale ablations, p. 9), and notes that final-answer checking credits solutions that reach the right answer by wrong reasoning (pp. 5, 8-9). Two limits matter for the revision but do not make the sentence wrong: in the paper, process supervision is the training signal given to a reward model (p. 3, section 2.1), not a way of evaluating a model's trace against a reference; and its step labels came from human labelers because there was no simple way to automate process supervision (p. 3). Separately, the May reference entry is broken: of its 30 printed names only Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda, Edwards, Leike, Schulman and Sutskever are authors (p. 1); Baker, Lee and Cobbe are missing; and the venue is now ICLR 2024.

suggested_wording: Lightman et al. (2023) showed that process supervision, human feedback on each intermediate step, trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision on MATH, and released PRM800K, about 800,000 human step labels on model-generated MATH solutions, collected from human labelers because there was no simple way to automate process supervision.
facts_to_cite: Process supervision gives feedback on each intermediate reasoning step, outcome supervision only on the final result (p. 1); ORMs are trained on the final result, PRMs on each step (p. 2).

A process-supervised reward model solves 78.2% of a 500-problem representative subset of the MATH test set in best-of-1860 selection, against 72.4% for the outcome-supervised model and 69.6% for majority voting (p. 7; '78%' in the abstract, p. 1).
In controlled small-scale comparisons, with the large PRM as a synthetic labeler, process supervision outperforms both forms of outcome supervision at every data-collection scale (p. 9).

PRM800K holds about 800,000 step-level human labels (positive, negative or neutral) on 75,000 model-generated solutions to 12,000 MATH problems; 1,085,590 labels over 101,599 solutions before filtering (pp. 4, 17).
Step labels were collected from human labelers because 'there is no simple way to automate process supervision', whereas MATH final answers can be checked automatically (p. 3).

Final-answer grading gives positive labels to solutions that reach the correct answer through incorrect reasoning (pp. 5, 8); the authors call it 'a process which occasionally leads to misgraded solutions' (p. 5).

Labelers were given the ground-truth final answer but no reference solution, to avoid biasing them toward one solution path (p. 19); in phase 2 labelling stops at a solution's first negative step (pp. 6, 19).
Active learning, surfacing convincing wrong-answer solutions, made process supervision about 2.6 times more data-efficient (pp. 2, 9).
The PRM's advantage held on recent AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics and AMC10/12 questions: 72.9% against 63.8% (ORM) and 61.3% (majority voting), best-of-100 (p. 10, Table 1).
The authors state that it is unknown how broadly the results generalise beyond mathematics (p. 11).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the premise that a correct final answer can hide a wrong step and that judging steps is more informative than judging answers (pp. 5, 8-9), and the step as the unit of judgement. Lacks: generated instances (MATH problems are static; only solutions are sampled); gold reference traces (labels are human verdicts on model solutions, and labelers saw no reference solution, p. 19); step-level evaluation of models (the step labels train a reward model, which is then scored by best-of-N final-answer accuracy, p. 3); an engineering domain (mathematics, with a small AP Physics and Chemistry OOD set, p. 10); and validation of an evaluator against experts (labelers are screened at 75% agreement with researchers' labels, pp. 17-18, but no agreement statistics are reported). EngTrace's link to it is indirect: PRMs are a baseline EngTrace measured (state brief section 3), and one of them, VersaPRM, is a LoRA on a Llama PRM800K model.
notes: Batch V question: this is the anchor for the planned paragraph on process supervision. It bears on that paragraph in four ways: (1) it defines outcome and process supervision (pp. 1-2); (2) it shows that step-level human labels train better verifiers than final-answer labels on MATH (pp. 7, 9); (3) it reports that final-answer checking misgrades right-answer, wrong-reasoning solutions (pp. 5, 8), the problem EngTrace measured directly (93 of 228 correct-answer traces in X1 contain an incorrect step, state brief section 3); (4) it released PRM800K (p. 17), from which one of EngTrace's measured PRM baselines descends. It says nothing about LLM judges. Given that the evaluator is now deterministic checks plus a residual MiMo judge, and that the PRMs are measured baselines outside the stack, the revised text may cite it for the outcome/process distinction, for the right-answer/wrong-step motivation, and as the source of PRM800K. It should not be cited as a precedent for EngTrace's checking method: in the paper, process supervision is a training signal for a reward model (p. 3, section 2.1), and the labels are human verdicts made without a reference solution (p. 19). One contrast is fair to draw: Lightman et al. needed human labelers because 'there is no simple way to automate process supervision' (p. 3), whereas EngTrace's templates compute the intermediate values (milestones) a correct trace must state. That contrast covers numerical steps only, since the deterministic checks catch none of the 60 planted conceptual errors (state brief section 3). Terminology: EngTrace's title phrase 'verifiable process supervision' uses the term for evaluation; a reviewer who knows this paper may object, so the revision could say 'step-level evaluation' where it means evaluation. Reference entry: regenerate it (30 printed names, 23 of them not authors, for example Mesnard, Khorrami and Zaremba; Baker, Lee and Cobbe missing; venue ICLR 2024 rather than arXiv). Internal inconsistency in the paper: the OOD set is '224 STEM questions' in the text, but Table 1 totals 234 (p. 10).
